newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil lower house set for key civil service vote.
newsitem.headline: Brazil lower house set for key civil service vote.

text.p: Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, who turned 66 on Wednesday, is waiting to see if the Chamber of Deputies will give him the birthday present he most wants -- a key victory in his civil service reform battle.
The lower house of Congress was due to vote in the late afternoon or early evening on an opposition amendment that would allow civil servants to retain their lifetime job guarantees.
The government has delayed the vote for nearly two months, fearing it might not muster the three-fifths majority needed to kill the amendment, which could render the reform meaningless.
But Legislative whips said the vote would take place Wednesday. "We vote today," said Deputy Inocencio Oliveira, the lower house leader of the government-allied Liberal Front Party (PFL).

Many Congress watchers believe the government will likely lose the vote because a majority of deputies, with their eyes on next year's elections, do not want to back a measure that would lead to thousands of job cuts.

To make matters worse, many lawmakers from Brazil's north and northeast were reported to have remained in their home areas this week to take part in annual holidays celebrating the feast days of St John and St Peter.

In an article in the newspaper O Globo entitled "Expected Defeat," columnist Franklin Martins said failure to crush the amendment would represent the biggest blow to Cardoso since he took office in January 1995.
"The essence of the reform will have been lost, and it will be impossible to carry out change in the current structure of the public sector," Martins said.

The civil service reform bill is intended to streamline the public sector, principally by allowing federal and local governments to dismiss workers who at present cannot be fired. Many states and municipalities spend about 80 percent of their receipts on payrolls. A few spend more than 100 percent.
But the reform, as well as another bill to modernize Brazil's pension system currently in the Senate, may have to wait until after the next Congress is seated in 1999.

The presidential, congressional and state gubernatorial elections scheduled for October 1998 are fast becoming the main item on the political agenda, making it difficult for the government to keep control of its volatile, multiparty alliance.
In an interview this week, Cardoso sought to focus attention back on the civil service reform bill and another piece of legislation to reverse a deficit in the pensions system.
"The reforms are essential and I will fight for them until the very end," he told Globo television, saying the proposal to end lifetime job guarantees was "an item of public morality."
Investors have already less optimistic of reform being approved in the near future, said Tulio Vera, a managing director with Bear Stearns & Co. in New York.

"We're at a very critical junction of the whole process of reforms," Vera said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television. "What we're likely to see if it doesn't go well in the next few days is a gradual corrosion of emphasis given by the government for reforms."
O Globo columnist Franklin went further, suggesting the government might scrap the reform altogether and replace it with a narrowly focused bill containing only a handful of points.
